Chapter 2: The Shadow of Political Upheaval
When a country’s caught in the chaos of political upheaval, those waves don’t just stay in the big cities—they reach every corner, even the quietest villages. Here, the Cultural Revolution isn’t some distant event you hear about on the radio. It’s woven into daily life. Slogans painted on walls, loudspeakers blaring out messages, meetings that seem to stretch on forever—all of it seeps into the neighborhood, into homes, into routines.
For families with the wrong background, the pressure never lets up. Take the boy’s family, for example. They carry that “landlord” label, and it’s like they’re living under a magnifying glass. Every move is watched. Every word is weighed. There’s this constant feeling that trouble could come from anywhere—a neighbor’s comment, a careless slip, or just a change in the political winds.
School isn’t exactly a safe haven, either. The boy feels the sting of that scrutiny from classmates who are quick to use his family’s status against him, especially when playground spats break out. Even teachers tread carefully. Some risk small acts of kindness when nobody’s looking, while others keep their distance, afraid that just being near him could put them in danger too.
His father’s situation is even tougher. Once respected for his knowledge, now he’s eyed with suspicion. He’s dragged into endless meetings, forced to confess to things he didn’t do, and made to stand before the village as others publicly denounce him. The humiliation is sharp and very public, but somehow, he faces it with a quiet strength. At home, he tries to protect his kids from the worst of it, but the strain is written clearly in the lines on his face.
The boy’s mother, though—she’s practical and resourceful. She finds clever ways to keep the family going. Bartering with neighbors, stretching every scrap of food, and teaching her children when it’s safe to speak and when it’s wiser to stay silent. Survival isn’t just about working hard—it’s about reading the room and knowing when to keep your head down.
The boy learns fast. He gets good at sensing the mood, figuring out when trouble’s brewing. He watches as some families are targeted, their homes searched, their possessions taken away. It becomes painfully clear—safety is never guaranteed, and the rules can change in an instant.
Still, life pushes forward. The fields need tending, animals have to be fed, and somehow the kids find ways to play. There are stolen moments of laughter, shared meals, small celebrations. And it’s in these fleeting moments that you really see it—people clinging to their humanity, even when everything around them feels so dark.
Over the years, the political climate does start to shift. The worst of the violence fades. But those scars? They linger. The boy’s family is still marked by their past, still watched, still struggling to belong. Yet, there’s a quiet sense that maybe—just maybe—the future could be different.
Through all of this, the boy carries away some powerful lessons. He witnesses resilience firsthand, understands the importance of dignity, and sees how people can support each other even when the world seems determined to pull them apart. These experiences shape him, give him a sense of purpose, and a determination to rise above the circumstances he was born into.
